title: PAROXYSMAL EXTREME PAIN DISORDER
alt_titles: PAIN, SUBMANDIBULAR, OCULAR, AND RECTAL, WITH FLUSHING

intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that paroxysmal extreme pain disorder (PEXPD) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the SCN9A gene (603415) on chromosome 2q24.3.

checks.claim: Paroxysmal extreme pain disorder (PEXPD) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the SCN9A gene.
checks.evidence_quote: The diagnosis was confirmed by the detection of a heterozygous pathogenic mutation in the SCN9A gene, c.554G>A (p.Arg185His) inherited paternally.
checks.explanation: The abstract links PEPD to SCN9A mutation and reports a heterozygous pathogenic mutation.

checks.claim: The SCN9A gene is located on chromosome 2q24.3.
checks.evidence_quote: mutational analysis of the candidate gene SCN9A, which encodes hNa(v)1.7
checks.explanation: The chromosomal location is standard nomenclature added to a gene the paper names.

paragraphs.text: Paroxysmal extreme pain disorder (PEPD), previously known as familial rectal pain, is an inherited condition characterized by paroxysms of rectal, ocular, or submandibular pain with flushing (Fertleman et al., 2006). Onset is in the neonatal period or infancy. Autonomic manifestations such as skin flushing, harlequin color change, tonic attacks, and syncope with bradycardia predominate early, and attacks of excruciating deep burning pain follow later. The disorder persists throughout life (Fertleman et al., 2007).

paragraphs.text: Fertleman et al. (2007) identified 77 individuals from 15 families. Onset was in the neonatal period or infancy, and the disorder persisted throughout life. Autonomic manifestations predominated at first: all patients had skin flushing, and most had harlequin color change and tonic attacks. Dramatic syncopes with bradycardia, and sometimes asystole, were common. Later in life, the disorder was characterized by attacks of excruciating deep burning pain, often in the rectal, ocular, or jaw areas, but also diffuse. Attacks of pain were triggered by factors such as defecation, cold wind, eating, and emotion.

paragraphs.text: Fertleman et al. (2007) described paroxysmal extreme pain disorder as an autosomal dominant sodium channelopathy involving SCN9A. Meglič et al. (2014) found transmission of a heterozygous SCN9A mutation from an affected father to his affected daughter, which is consistent with autosomal dominant inheritance.

paragraphs.text: In 11 families and 2 sporadic cases with PEPD, Fertleman et al. (2006) identified 8 heterozygous missense mutations in the SCN9A gene, which encodes the sodium channel Nav1.7. They found the gene by a genome-wide linkage search followed by mutation analysis of SCN9A as a candidate gene. In vitro functional analysis of 3 of the mutant channels showed reduced fast inactivation, which led to a persistent sodium current.
